transport: CONTRADICTED between sources. Most community configs use RTU-over-TCP (and sometimes plain Modbus TCP) to port 8088, slave ID 1. One openHAB thread reports the adapter answering on port 502 and plain Modbus TCP failing outright, requiring a virtual COM port or a separate RTU-to-TCP gateway. Both are recorded; neither is vendor-stated.
blocks: Same as epever-tracer-a — the adapter tunnels the controller's own register map unchanged. Community configs show decimal 12544 (0x3100), 12545 (0x3101), 12546 (0x3102), 12558 (0x310E), 12560 (0x3110), 12570 (0x311A), 13082 (0x331A), 12800–12802 (0x3200–0x3202).

models.name: (EPEVER WiFi 2.4G RJ45 A / DB9 B are the current equivalents)

sharedMapEvidence: Not a distinct register map — a transport adapter. It plugs into the controller's RS-485 RJ45 and re-serves the same Modbus frames over the LAN, which is why the register numbers in every community config decode to the epever-tracer-a addresses (12544 = 0x3100, 13082 = 0x331A, 12570 = 0x311A). gotchas: CONTRADICTION on the port and the framing: 8088 with RTU-over-TCP in the Home Assistant configs, 502 with plain Modbus TCP failing in the openHAB thread. Nothing vendor-stated settles it. Probe both before wiring a driver to either.

The adapter occupies the controller's single RS-485 port. It is an alternative to a wired gateway, not an addition to one — and it is a Modbus master while the app is polling, so the collision hazard is the same as the MT50's.
No vendor document defines the network side. Everything about port, framing, and behaviour here is community-derived; the datasheet describes the product, not a protocol.
A LAN-attached bridge with an unauthenticated Modbus port and a web dashboard on port 80 is a different security posture from a serial cable. Worth deciding deliberately rather than by default.
